extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of Plato, classical literature, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for judging poetry, myth/storytelling, and rhetoric as found in Plato (and in general literary practice), including what makes art morally and aesthetically valuable and which storytelling devices create credibility and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art (and politics) must be true; bring order out of disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: "Art then must be true, and politics must be true, and the life of man must be true and not a seeming or sham. In all of them order has to be brought out of disorder, truth out of error and falsehood."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The highest aim of artistic and political activity is truth and moral order: art should correct error and falsehood and produce the greatest improvement of man. Plato implies an ultimate triumph of truth and right; art should not be mere seeming or sophistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: True office of the poet/writer of fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: "The true office of a poet or writer of fiction is not merely to give amusement, or to be the expression of the feelings of mankind..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet should teach and uplift: speak of themes above ordinary life, speak of them in a deeper and tenderer way so as to awaken feeling in others, clothe noblest truths with beauty, invest familiar principles with new dignity, reveal men's nature rather than disguise it, and be his own critic. Examples cited: Goethe, Wordsworth, Greek dramatists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should elevate pleasure (use higher pleasure to raise men)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Neither is the element of pleasure to be excluded. For when we substitute a higher pleasure for a lower we raise men in the scale of existence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasure in art is permissible but should be ordered toward higher goods; novels and poetry can form ideals of social life and influence moral improvement when they substitute higher for lower pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern — poetry as mere plaything or flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern poetry as 'a sort of plaything, or ... a flattery, a sophistry, or sham' that seeks only to gratify taste or exhibit verbal skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning signs of inferior poetry: technical 'savoir faire' without higher spirit; idealizing the sensual; forgetting measure and order; prioritizing what is strongest over what is truest; working out some heated fancy with incongruity; being dominated by borrowed or fashionable words. Such art lacks healing or life-giving influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as master of words; measure and order required
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet 'is not the master of his words, but his words ... have the better of him' is a defect; true art 'should bring order out of disorder' and 'be pursued only with a view to the improvement of the citizens.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good poets control language and structure; they maintain measure and order, select language that strengthens feeling and moral insight, and avoid loose, overheated, or incoherent expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storytelling devices that create credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "The art of making stories of ghosts and apparitions credible is said to consist in the manner of telling them. The effect is gained by many literary and conversational devices, such as the previous raising of curiosity, the mention of little circumstances, simplicity, picturesqueness, the naturalness of the occasion, and the like."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make myths, legends, or ghost-stories convincing, employ preliminary curiosity, small concrete details, simple and picturesque language, and a natural-sounding occasion; these devices increase verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of myths/parables as substitute and reform of mythology
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato's myths are 'a substitute for poetry and mythology; and they are also a reform of mythology'—simple in style, employing sacred/familiar names to gain authority, and presented as the best that can be said about a future life rather than literal revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myths should be presented with simplicity and authoritative touch (e.g., use of familiar sacred names) while avoiding dogmatism; they work when used at the limits of rational knowledge to convey moral truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous images and repeated figures (use sparingly; create life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato employs continuous images (e.g., the sun, bees, composite animal) that recur and bind argument to picture; 'the striking image ... is not forgotten, but is quickly caught up, and alluded to again and again.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recurring images can give unity and force to a work, making it lively and memorable, but overworking a single figure or repeating it too often risks prosy monotony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style: homeliness, simplicity, conversational ease
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato's descriptions have 'a greater life and reality than is to be found in any modern writing. This is due to their homeliness and simplicity... In the myths and parables of Plato the ease and grace of conversation is not forgotten: they are spoken, not written words.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective literary style may combine spoken conversational grace with philosophical depth; homely, simple diction and natural speech rhythms can produce vivid, convincing description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced use of modes: visible (sense) and unseen (abstract)
rubrics_metrics.description: A great writer 'knows how to strike both these chords, sometimes remaining within the sphere of the visible, and then again comprehending a wider range and soaring to the abstract and universal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should be able to move between concrete sensory imagery and abstract thought appropriately; mixing the two can be powerful, but success depends on the writer's genius and familiarity of associations used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of rhetoric (distinctive criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetoric is 'with discourse'—it makes men able to speak and to understand what they speak of, but it is not equivalent to the technical knowledge of other arts; unlike other arts, rhetoric 'works and takes effect only through the medium of discourse' and does not involve an external action of the hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating rhetoric, distinguish it from technical arts (medicine, gymnastic): rhetoric's domain is persuasive discourse in matters where action is effected through speech alone. Clarify whether rhetoric's aim is mere persuasion or the teaching of truth, and note Socratic critique that praising an art is not the same as defining its nature.
